# AGENTS.md

Guidance for AI agents working in the **openkit** repository.

## What this repo is

`openkit` is an OpenCode V2 plugin that hosts independently toggleable items
grouped into **categories**: tools and skills. The framework (config,
category engine, contracts) is the product; items are added on top. Every
category is one `KitCategory` descriptor consumed by the generic engine, so
config resolution, registration/isolation, and `/kit` are shared. One
tool ships today: `context-injections`
(`src/tools/context-injections/index.ts`, on by default; injects built-in behavioral
rules, each individually toggleable, plus your own instructions; a rule needing a
tool the request lacks is skipped). The `hello`
example at `src/tools/hello/index.ts` is not registered at runtime. Twenty-one
skills ship today, all enabled by default: `english-writing-assistant`
(`src/skills/english-writing-assistant/SKILL.md`, model-visible), `sdd-flow`
(`src/skills/sdd-flow/SKILL.md`, registered `autoinvoke: false`, invoked with
`@sdd-flow`; a self-contained spec-driven development orchestrator that
brainstorms approaches before the interview for architectural work, then
executes approved specs in batches (one step, or independent steps in parallel)
with a per-step gate, composing the kit's own `interview`, `research`,
`code-review`, `codebase-design`, `using-git-worktrees`, and
`dispatching-parallel-agents` skills and naming `to-spec` for drafting the
initial spec), `interview`
(`src/skills/interview/SKILL.md`, model-visible; aligns on design before
implementation), `skill-recipe` (`src/skills/skill-recipe/SKILL.md`, registered
`autoinvoke: false`, the authoring recipe invoked with `@skill-recipe`),
`research` (`src/skills/research/SKILL.md`, model-visible; cited findings from
primary sources), `handoff` (`src/skills/handoff/SKILL.md`, registered
`autoinvoke: false`, invoked with `@handoff`; compacts the conversation into a
resumable document), `code-review` (`src/skills/code-review/SKILL.md`,
model-visible; reviews a change along Standards and Spec), `diagnosing-bugs`
(`src/skills/diagnosing-bugs/SKILL.md`, model-visible; root-causes a bug from
evidence before changing production code), `verification`
(`src/skills/verification/SKILL.md`, model-visible; proves a completion claim
against the current tree before reporting success), `prototype`
(`src/skills/prototype/SKILL.md`, model-visible; builds throwaway code to resolve
one design uncertainty), `retro` (`src/skills/retro/SKILL.md`, registered
`autoinvoke: false`, invoked with `@retro`; turns a finished session's friction
into proposed environment changes), `finishing-a-branch`
(`src/skills/finishing-a-branch/SKILL.md`, registered `autoinvoke: false`, invoked
with `@finishing-a-branch`; lands completed work safely or leaves it deliberately
in place), `dispatching-parallel-agents`
(`src/skills/dispatching-parallel-agents/SKILL.md`, model-visible; delegates one
agent per independent task and runs them concurrently), `using-git-worktrees`
(`src/skills/using-git-worktrees/SKILL.md`, model-visible; sets up or verifies an
isolated workspace before feature work), `writing-for-agents`
(`src/skills/writing-for-agents/SKILL.md`, model-visible; writes agent-facing
documents so the agent lands on the intended behavior), and `codebase-design`
(`src/skills/codebase-design/SKILL.md`, model-visible; designs deep modules
behind clean seams), `improve-codebase-architecture`
(`src/skills/improve-codebase-architecture/SKILL.md`, registered
`autoinvoke: false`, invoked with `@improve-codebase-architecture`; surveys a
codebase read-only for deepening opportunities),
`to-spec` (`src/skills/to-spec/SKILL.md`, registered `autoinvoke: false`, invoked
with `@to-spec`; distills the current conversation into a written spec),
`wizard` (`src/skills/wizard/SKILL.md`, model-visible; builds a guided
interactive script for steps only a human can take), `router`
(`src/skills/router/SKILL.md`, registered `autoinvoke: false`, invoked with
`@router`; points a request at the one kit skill or flow that fits), and
`diagnosing-sessions` (`src/skills/diagnosing-sessions/SKILL.md`, registered
`autoinvoke: false`, invoked with `@diagnosing-sessions`; forensically explains
why a past session went wrong).

## Commands

Prepend Bun to your `PATH` (`~/.bun/bin`) if needed.

```bash
bun run typecheck   # must pass before you commit
bun test            # must pass before you commit
bun scripts/doctor.ts             # maintainer health check
bun scripts/skill-source.ts check # generated skill drift
```

There is no build step: the plugin is the TypeScript source, transpiled by Bun
at load.

Run a single test file with `bun test tests/unit/<file>.test.ts`.

## Layout

```text
src/
  plugin.ts             # plugin entry (id + setup) and bootstrap/lifecycle orchestration
  catalog.ts            # assembles categories from the descriptors
  constants.ts          # shared PLUGIN_ID
  categories/           # tool and skill descriptors
  operations/           # shared list/toggle/config ops used by /kit
  commands/             # the /kit slash command (adapter over operations)
  config/               # discover, load, merge, effective, validate, edit, coerce, types
  core/                 # category contract + engine, item contracts, kit API, context, testing fakes
  tools/<id>/index.ts   # one folder per tool
  tools/index.ts        # explicit barrel with <kit:tools> markers
  skills/<id>/SKILL.md  # one folder per skill (+ optional support files)
  skills/index.ts       # explicit barrel with <kit:skills> markers
index.js                # package plugin entry -> src/plugin.ts
openkit.schema.json     # JSON schema for openkit.jsonc
docs/                   # examples (not published)
scripts/                # repo tooling (not published): doctor, skill-source
skill-sources/          # vendored skill sources (dev-only, not published)
tests/unit, tests/integration # behavior tests
.opencode/INSTALL.md    # agent-driven install for consumers
```

## Ground rules

- **Match the real behavior.** `README.md` and `.opencode/INSTALL.md` must
  describe what `src/` actually does. The user-facing interface is `/kit`;
  maintainer tooling lives under `scripts/` and is not shipped.
- **Isolation is a hard requirement.** Every item's registration runs in
  try/catch; failures become `degraded` entries and an item's partial
  registrations are disposed. Never let one item break the kit or its siblings.
- **Config edits preserve comments.** Use the `jsonc-parser` helpers in
  `src/config/edit.ts`. Do not rewrite config with `JSON.stringify`.
- **Explicit registration.** Items are discovered from typed barrels
  (`src/tools/index.ts`, `src/skills/index.ts`), not
  runtime globbing. Keep the `<kit:tools>` and `<kit:skills>` markers intact; add
  new entries between them manually.
- **Tests accompany behavior.** Use `createFakeContext` from
  `src/core/testing.ts` for harness-style assertions. Add tests for new config
  precedence, registry behavior, `/kit` output, and tool registration.
- **The host contract is pinned, not assumed.** `@opencode/plugin` is an exact
  devDependency, and `tests/unit/context-conformance.test.ts` proves at compile
  time that the real V2 `Context` satisfies `KitContext`. The import is
  type-only, so the published plugin still loads without the package. When
  adopting a newer OpenCode, bump the pin, rerun `bun run typecheck`, and fix
  whatever the contract check surfaces; update the `README.md` requirement to
  match.
- **Conventional Commits.** Use `feat:`, `fix:`, `docs:`, `test:`, `chore:`.
  Run `bun run typecheck && bun test` before committing.
- **No build step — the TypeScript source is the artifact.** Consumers install
  directly from GitHub and Bun (OpenCode's runtime) transpiles `src/plugin.ts`
  on load, so there is no `dist/`. Keep `src` in `package.json` `files`, and keep
  `index.js`/`main` pointing at the TS entry.
- **Do not name scripts `build`, `prepare`, `prepack`, or `postinstall`.** For
  git-installed dependencies Bun runs (and, for untrusted git deps, blocks)
  those lifecycle names, which makes `opencode plugin add <git spec>` fail with
  `git dep preparation failed`. Keep the build step out of `package.json`
  entirely (there is none).

## Configuration model (memorize this)

Locations:

- Global: `~/.config/opencode/openkit.jsonc`
- Project: `<project>/.opencode/openkit.jsonc`, discovered upward from the
  instance directory, nearest wins.

Precedence, low → high:

```text
item defaultSettings (settings-bearing categories)
  < global config < project config (farther→nearer)
    < opencode.json plugins[].options
```

`settings` deep-merge; `enabled` replaces; arrays replace. Config stays
category-keyed (`tools`, `skills`).

## Adding a tool

1. Create `src/tools/my-tool/index.ts` and add it to `src/tools/index.ts`
   between the `<kit:tools>` markers.
2. Implement `register(ctx, settings, kit)` in `src/tools/my-tool/index.ts`.
3. Add tests.
4. Add an example entry to `docs/examples/openkit.jsonc`.
5. `bun run typecheck && bun test`.

`defineTool` defaults `defaultEnabled` to `true`; set it to `false` for a tool
that should stay off until config enables it.

## Adding a skill

Prefer `@skill-recipe` (`src/skills/skill-recipe/SKILL.md`) to derive a skill
from a brief plus source skills: it drafts in the kit house style and adds the
barrel entry. The steps below are the manual equivalent.

1. Create `src/skills/my-skill/SKILL.md` and add an entry to
   `src/skills/index.ts` between the `<kit:skills>` markers.
2. Write `src/skills/my-skill/SKILL.md` (frontmatter `name`/`description` plus
   the instruction body; add support files beside it as needed).
3. Add tests.
4. Add an example entry to `docs/examples/openkit.jsonc`.
5. `bun run typecheck && bun test`.

A skill is declarative: a directory plus one barrel line, no code. `defineSkill`
defaults `defaultEnabled` to `true`; pass `autoinvoke: false` to hide it from the
model's advertised list while keeping it loadable by id (`@my-skill`).

See `CONTRIBUTING.md` for the full contributor workflow.

name: code-review
description: Use when reviewing a change (a diff, a PR, or a completed task) before it merges, and when receiving review feedback on your own work. Trigger on requests to review a branch, PR, or diff, and when handed review comments to act on.
---

# Code Review

Review a change along two independent axes, Standards and Spec, so neither masks the other. On the receiving side, verify every finding against the code and the rule it cites before acting on it.

## Overview

A code review answers two separate questions about a change: does it follow this repo's standards, and does it implement what was asked. A change can pass one axis and fail the other, so the two are reviewed independently and reported side by side, never merged into a single ranking. Findings carry a severity: Critical, Important, or Minor. Reviewing and receiving are the same discipline from opposite ends. Both run on evidence over impression, and both verify a claim about the code against the code before accepting or acting on it.

## When to Use

- A change is about to merge and needs review: a diff, a branch, a PR, or a completed task.
- The user asks to review work, or to review the changes since a fixed point.
- You receive review feedback on your own change and need to act on it.
- A finding is unclear or technically questionable and needs verification rather than agreement.

## Process

### Reviewing a change

#### 1. Pin the fixed point and read the diff

Take the fixed point the user gives (a commit, branch, tag, or merge-base). Compare against it with a three-dot diff so the comparison runs against the merge-base, and note the commits in range. Confirm the ref resolves and the diff is non-empty before going further.

**An empty diff is the finding.** If there is no change, report that plainly and stop. Never invent findings to fill a review.

#### 2. Gather the two contracts

- **Standards**: the repo's documented coding standards, conventions, and contributing rules.
- **Spec**: the originating requirements, issue, plan, or brief. If none exists, the Spec axis reports "no spec available" instead of guessing.

#### 3. Review both axes in parallel

Run the two axes independently, in parallel when the harness supports it, so neither pollutes the other's context. If the harness has no parallel path, run them in sequence and keep the findings separate.

**Standards axis.** Per file and hunk, report:

- every place the change violates a documented standard, citing the standard (file and the rule);
- judgement-call smells (naming, duplication, feature envy, primitive obsession, and similar) named as heuristics, never as hard violations;
- a documented repo standard overrides any baseline heuristic, and rules that tooling already enforces are skipped.

**Spec axis.** Report:

- requirements the spec asked for that are missing or partial;
- behaviour in the change that was not asked for (scope creep);
- requirements that look implemented but where the implementation looks wrong.

Quote the spec line for each finding. If the spec is missing, skip this axis and note that in the report.

#### 4. Report side by side

Present the two axes under separate headings, verbatim or lightly cleaned. Do not merge or rerank across axes: the separation exists so one axis cannot mask the other. Label every finding Critical, Important, or Minor. End with a one-line summary of the finding count per axis and the worst issue within each axis. Do not pick a single winner across axes.

### Receiving review feedback

#### 1. Read and understand

Read the feedback in full before reacting. Restate each requirement in your own words. If any item is unclear, ask before implementing anything: related items mean partial understanding leads to a wrong fix.

#### 2. Verify each finding

For every finding, check it against the actual code and the rule it cites. Confirm the code behaves as the finding claims and that the cited rule applies here. Do not accept a finding on authority, and do not reject one to avoid the work.

#### 3. Apply, reject, or find a better fix

For each finding, either apply it, reject it with a technical reason, or find a better fix, and state the reason. When a suggestion is wrong for this codebase, push back with technical reasoning and evidence (code, tests), not defensiveness. When you were wrong, say so factually and move on.

#### 4. Order the work

Clarify anything unclear first. Then fix blocking issues (breaks, security), then simple fixes, then complex ones. Verify after each fix.

## Gates

- **Empty diff reported as such.** No change means no findings; findings are never invented.
- **Two axes, reported separately.** Standards and Spec stay distinct and are never merged or reranked across.
- **Every finding cites its contract.** A standards finding cites the standard (file and rule); a spec finding quotes the spec line.
- **Severity assigned.** Each finding is Critical, Important, or Minor.
- **Findings verified before acted on.** On the receiving side, each finding is checked against the code and the rule it cites before it is applied or rejected.
- **Rejection carries a reason.** A rejected finding comes with the technical reason it does not apply.

## Anti-patterns

- Inventing findings when the diff is empty.
- Merging the two axes into a single ranking, letting one mask the other.
- Reporting a standards breach without citing the standard, or a spec gap without quoting the spec.
- Treating a judgement-call smell as a hard violation, or overriding a documented repo standard with a heuristic.
- Accepting review feedback on authority without verifying it against the code.
- Rejecting a finding to avoid the work, or agreeing performatively to keep the peace.
- Implementing a batch of feedback before clarifying the items that are unclear.

name: codebase-design
description: Use when designing modules and interfaces, or reviewing a structure for depth and locality. Trigger on deciding where a seam goes, shaping a module's interface, judging whether a module is deep or shallow, or making code more testable or navigable. Do not use for routine implementation inside an already-settled design.
---

# Codebase Design

Design **deep modules**: a lot of behavior behind a small interface, placed at a clean seam, testable through that interface. The aim is leverage for callers, locality for maintainers, and testability for everyone.

## Overview

A module is anything with an interface and an implementation, at any scale: a function, a class, a package, or a tier-spanning slice. Its **interface** is everything a caller must know to use it correctly: the type signature, plus invariants, ordering constraints, error modes, required configuration, and performance characteristics. Its **implementation** is the body of code inside.

A module is **deep** when a large amount of behavior sits behind a small interface, and **shallow** when the interface is nearly as complex as the implementation. Depth is leverage: more capability per unit of interface a caller or test has to learn. It is also locality: change, bugs, knowledge, and verification concentrate in one place instead of spreading across callers.

Depth is a property of the interface, not the implementation. A deep module can be internally composed of small, swappable parts; those parts are simply not part of the interface.

## When to Use

- You are designing a module's interface or deciding what it should expose.
- You are reviewing a structure for depth and locality, or for shallow sprawl.
- You are deciding where a seam goes, or whether one is warranted at all.
- You want the code to be more testable or easier for a reader to navigate.
- You are judging whether an existing module earns its keep.

## Process

### 1. Name the module and its interface

State what the module is and everything a caller must know to use it. Include the non-type facts: invariants, ordering, error modes, configuration, and performance. If the interface cannot be written down, it is not yet designed.

### 2. Apply the deletion test

Imagine deleting the module. If the complexity vanishes, it was a pass-through. If the complexity reappears across N callers, it was earning its keep. A module that only forwards calls is a shallow one.

### 3. Prefer depth

Ask whether the interface can be smaller: fewer methods, simpler parameters, more complexity hidden inside. Move behavior behind the interface rather than widening it. Internal parts stay private even when they are individually small and swappable.

### 4. Place the seam deliberately

A **seam** is a place where behavior can change without editing in that place: the location at which the interface lives. Where the seam goes is its own decision, separate from what goes behind it. Put it where variation is real, not where it is imagined.

### 5. Introduce a seam only when something varies across it

An **adapter** is a concrete thing that satisfies the interface at a seam. One adapter means a hypothetical seam. Two adapters means a real one. Do not introduce a seam unless something actually varies across it.

### 6. Design the interface as the test surface

Callers and tests cross the same seam. If you want to test past the interface, the module is probably the wrong shape. Make testing natural: accept dependencies instead of creating them, return results instead of producing side effects, and keep the surface small.

### 7. Optimize for locality

Keep change, knowledge, and verification in one place. Fix once, fixed everywhere. A design that scatters a single rule across many callers costs every future change.

## Gates

- **Depth is a property of the interface.** A large implementation behind a small interface is deep; an interface as complex as its implementation is shallow.
- **The interface is the test surface.** Callers and tests cross the same seam. Testing past the interface signals the wrong shape.
- **One adapter is a hypothetical seam.** A seam is introduced only when something actually varies across it; two adapters make it real.
- **The deletion test passes.** Deleting the module would scatter its complexity across callers, not remove it.
- **Locality holds.** Change and verification concentrate in one place rather than spreading across callers.
- **Dependencies are accepted, not created, and results are returned, not produced as side effects.**

## Anti-patterns

- Shallow sprawl: a large interface over a thin implementation that mostly passes calls through.
- Widening the interface to avoid hiding complexity inside.
- Introducing a seam for a single adapter, when nothing varies across it yet.
- Testing past the interface because the module is the wrong shape.
- Creating dependencies inside a module instead of accepting them.
- Mutating shared state as a side effect instead of returning a result.
- Spreading one rule across many callers instead of keeping it local.

name: diagnosing-bugs
description: Use when a bug, failing test, or unexpected behavior must be root-caused before fixing. Trigger on reports of something broken, throwing, failing, slow, or otherwise misbehaving, and when a fix is proposed but the cause is not yet known.
---

# Diagnosing Bugs

Find the root cause before changing production code. A bug you cannot reproduce is a bug you cannot fix, and a fix without a demonstrated cause is a guess that will move the symptom rather than remove it.

## Overview

A hard bug has a cause, and the cause is reachable by evidence. The work is a gated loop: build a signal that goes red on this bug, shrink it to the smallest failing case, test one falsifiable hypothesis at a time, and only then change production code. The loop is the skill; the fix is mechanical once the cause is demonstrated. Redact secrets before showing any command, output, or captured artifact, and build loops against environment variables so credentials stay in the environment rather than in the transcript.

## When to Use

- A bug, failing test, or unexpected behavior must be fixed and the cause is not known.
- Something is broken, throwing, failing, slow, or producing wrong output.
- A fix is proposed, or one already failed, before the cause was demonstrated.
- The issue seems simple, you are under time pressure, or you have already tried multiple fixes.

## Process

### 1. Build a feedback loop that goes red

Produce one command, already run at least once, that drives the bug's code path and asserts the user's exact symptom, so it can go red on this bug and green once fixed. It must be deterministic, fast (seconds), and runnable unattended. Prefer a failing test at the seam that reaches the bug; fall back to an HTTP script, a CLI invocation against a fixture, a headless browser script, a replayed trace, or a throwaway harness.

Tighten the loop once it exists: make it faster, make the signal sharper (assert the specific symptom, not "did not crash"), and make it more deterministic (pin time, seed randomness, freeze the network). For non-deterministic bugs, stop chasing a clean repro and raise the reproduction rate until the bug is debuggable. If you genuinely cannot build a loop, stop and say so: list what you tried and ask for access to the environment, a redacted captured artifact, or permission to add temporary instrumentation. Do not hypothesize without a loop.

### 2. Reproduce and minimize

Run the loop and watch it go red. Confirm the failure is the one the user described, not a nearby failure, and capture the exact symptom so a later phase can verify the fix addresses it.

Then shrink the repro to the smallest scenario that still goes red. Cut inputs, callers, config, data, and steps one at a time, re-running the loop after each cut, and keep only what is load-bearing. Done when removing any remaining element makes the loop go green. A minimal repro shrinks the hypothesis space and becomes the regression test.

### 3. Form one hypothesis at a time

State a single falsifiable hypothesis: "If X is the cause, then changing Y will make the bug disappear, and changing Z will make it worse." If you cannot state the prediction, the hypothesis is a vibe; sharpen it or discard it. Test it by changing one variable at a time, using a debugger or REPL inspection first, then targeted logs at the boundaries that distinguish hypotheses. Never log everything and grep. Tag every temporary log with a unique prefix so cleanup is one search. For performance regressions, measure a baseline first, then bisect; do not reason from logs alone.

If the test does not confirm the hypothesis, form a new one and repeat. Do not stack fixes on top of an unconfirmed theory.

### 4. Verify the root cause before changing production code

This is the gate between diagnosis and repair. You may change production code only after the loop has demonstrated the root cause: the failing value or behavior is traced to the line that originates it, and you can explain why that line produces the symptom. Fix at the source, not at the point where the symptom appears. If three fixes have already failed, stop treating it as a hypothesis and question the design; each new fix revealing a new problem in a different place means the architecture, not the theory, is wrong.

### 5. Fix and verify

Turn the minimized repro into a regression test at a seam that exercises the real bug pattern at the call site, and confirm the new test fails on the unfixed tree. Apply a single fix that addresses the demonstrated cause, with no bundled cleanup. Confirm the test passes with the fix, that no other tests break, and re-run the original loop against the unminimized scenario. If the only available seam is too shallow to replicate the bug, say so: the missing seam is itself a finding about the codebase.

### 6. Clean up

Before declaring done, confirm the original repro no longer reproduces, the regression test passes or the absent seam is documented, every tagged instrument is removed, and throwaway prototypes are deleted. State the cause that turned out correct so the next debugger learns from it.

## Gates

- **No production change without a demonstrated root cause.** The cause is shown by the loop before code changes, never asserted from reading.
- **Reproduced and minimized first.** No hypothesizing until a red-capable loop exists and every remaining element is load-bearing.
- **One hypothesis at a time.** Each hypothesis is falsifiable and tested by changing one variable.
- **The fix is verified against the original symptom.** The unminimized repro is re-run after the fix, not just the new test.
- **Secrets are redacted.** Commands, outputs, and captured artifacts carry no credentials.
- **Instrumentation is removed.** Tagged logs and throwaway prototypes are gone before done.

## Anti-patterns

- Patching a symptom, or shipping any speculative fix, without a demonstrated root cause.
- Proposing a fix before the failing behavior is reproduced and its cause traced to its source.
- Reading code to build a theory before a red-capable loop exists.
- Changing several things at once, or stacking fixes on an unconfirmed hypothesis.
- Treating a nearby failure as the user's bug, or a different failure as the same one.
- Logging everything and grepping, or reasoning about performance from logs instead of a baseline measurement.
- Declaring done without re-running the original repro, or leaving tagged instrumentation behind.
- Showing credentials in a command, an output, or a captured artifact.

name: diagnosing-sessions
description: Use when explicitly invoked to investigate why a past agent session went wrong. Trigger on `@diagnosing-sessions`, or on requests to diagnose, review, or explain a session that stalled, repeated work, ignored a plan, ran over budget, or produced a poor result, for the current session or one named by id or path. Do not use to run the session's work or to change the environment.
---

# Diagnosing Sessions

Pin down what went wrong in a session, read the transcript on disk, and report what happened with evidence. You report; you do not fix.

## Overview

A session that went wrong leaves a transcript, and the transcript holds the answer. The work is forensic: scope the problem with the user, locate the session, read it, and report a timeline of what happened and where it diverged from intent. Every finding cites a `file:line` into the transcript, a log line, or a command you ran; every number comes from the transcript, never from memory. The skill is read-only. It reports findings and stops; it never silently "fixes" the session, edits a transcript, or changes the environment.

## When to Use

- The user invokes `@diagnosing-sessions`, or asks why a session went wrong.
- A session stalled, repeated work, ignored a plan, took too long, cost too much, or produced a poor result.
- The user wants a forensic timeline of a session, current or one named by id or path.
- The user wants a session's evidence turned into a bug report.

Do not use it to run the session's work, to redo what the session attempted, or to change the environment. It reports; the user decides what to change.

## Process

### 1. Scope the problem

Ask one question at a time until you can write a statement naming the session, the turn range if known, what the user expected, what happened, and the observable they care about (wall-clock, tokens, repeated actions, one specific action). "It took too long" is a complaint, not a problem statement. Note whether the goal is a bug report. Nothing below starts until this is answered; if the user is away, write the questions and stop.

### 2. Locate the transcript

Resolve each session to a verified absolute filesystem path. Confirm a past session by quoting its first prompt and timestamp, and list every candidate you rejected with the reason, or "none". Enumerate subagent transcripts. State the path where the report will live, and tell the user.

### 3. Read, then dispatch analysts

Read the region around the reported problem yourself first. Then dispatch one analyst subagent per dimension in parallel, each given the absolute transcript path and one dimension: timeline, plan adherence, repeated work, stumbles, quality evidence, request conflicts, cost and time. Split a dimension by turn range when the transcript is long. Discard any returned finding without a `file:line` citation.

Treat one transcript line as potentially huge; read session files in bounded chunks. Never modify, move, or delete a session file.

### 4. Report with citations

Write a timeline in order, mark where the session diverged from intent, and attach evidence to each finding as a `file:line` citation, a log line, or the command that produced it. State coverage plainly: what you read, and what you skipped. Show the report and give its path. Separate what the cited evidence proves from your own inference.

### 5. Offer follow-ups on request

Only when the user asks, offer to search for similar sessions or to draft a bug report from the findings. Do not act on those offers until the user asks. Pointing at a possible cause is the end of the report; a fix is the user's call.

## Gates

- **Every finding cites a source.** A finding carries a `file:line` citation into the transcript, a log line, or a command you ran. No citation, no finding.
- **Numbers are computed.** Time, tokens, and cost come from the transcript or a command you ran, never from memory.
- **Read-only.** Never modify, move, or delete a session file or any artifact under investigation.
- **Report, do not fix.** Findings are reported, not applied; the environment is not changed, and no fix is made without the user asking.
- **Human prompts only.** Hook output, system reminders, and tool results are not the user's words. In a subagent transcript, "user" is the parent agent.
- **Scope before analysis.** Nothing starts until the problem is scoped; if the user is away, write the questions and stop.

## Anti-patterns

- Editing, moving, or deleting a session file, or any artifact under investigation.
- Silently "fixing" the session or changing the environment instead of reporting.
- A finding with no `file:line`, log, or command citation.
- Recalling cost, time, or token numbers instead of computing them from the transcript.
- Sweeping the whole session before the problem is scoped.
- Treating hook output, system reminders, or tool results as the user's words.
- Naming a defect and proposing a fix when the user asked for a report.

name: dispatching-parallel-agents
description: Use when two or more independent tasks can be worked without shared state or sequential dependencies. Trigger on several unrelated failures, subsystems, or problem domains that can be investigated or implemented concurrently. Do not use when the tasks are related, share state, or need full-system context.
---

# Dispatching Parallel Agents

Delegate one agent per independent problem domain and let them run concurrently. Independence is the precondition; the coordinator keeps its own context for integration.

## Overview

When several tasks are genuinely independent, investigating or implementing them one at a time wastes wall-clock time that parallel work recovers. Delegate each task to an agent with isolated context, and construct exactly what that agent needs: it never inherits the coordinator's session or history. Focused, self-contained prompts keep each agent on its task, and dispatching them together lets them run at the same time. The coordinator keeps its own context free for the review and integration that follows.

The whole value depends on the tasks being independent. Work that is related, shares state, or needs the whole system stays with one agent or runs in sequence; parallelizing it multiplies confusion instead of saving time.

## When to Use

- For any non-trivial task, actively check whether two or more ready pieces can be worked without shared state or sequential dependencies.
- Several unrelated failures or subsystems each have their own cause.
- Each problem can be understood without context from the others.
- No shared state exists between the tasks: no common files, resources, or mutable state.
- The task domains are sufficiently understood to delegate safely. If they are not, do a bounded investigation first; then reassess whether independent investigations or work can proceed concurrently.

Do not parallelize when:

- A task depends on unfinished work; wait until its prerequisites are complete.
- The failures are related, so fixing one may fix the others; investigate them together first.
- The tasks share state, so agents would interfere by editing the same files or using the same resources.
- Understanding a task requires seeing the whole system rather than one domain.
- You are considering speculative implementation before enough investigation to establish independence. Independently scoped investigations may proceed concurrently when their scope and inputs are clear.

## Process

### 1. Identify independent domains

Group the work by what is broken, not by what is convenient. Name each domain and confirm it can be understood and changed on its own. If two domains touch the same code, resource, or decision, they are one domain, not two.

### 2. Write one focused prompt per domain

Give each agent a prompt that is:

- **Focused:** one clear problem domain, scoped to a single file, subsystem, or question.
- **Self-contained:** every piece of context the agent needs to understand the problem, pasted in. The agent does not see the coordinator's session, so the prompt carries the errors, test names, paths, and constraints.
- **Specific about output:** state exactly what the agent should return, such as a summary of the root cause and the changes made.
- **Constrained:** name what the agent must not touch, so it does not refactor beyond its scope.

### 3. Dispatch the ready set together

When at least two independent pieces are ready and the time saved justifies coordination, dispatch all of them in the same response so they run concurrently. Do not send one subagent at a time for work that is already known to be independent. For bounded queries that only need returned values, use batched tool calls instead of creating subagents. Never dispatch work across an approval gate or before its prerequisites are met.

### 4. Review and integrate

When the agents return:

- Read each summary to understand what changed.
- Check for conflicts, especially agents that edited the same code.
- Run the full suite so the changes are verified together, not just in isolation.
- Spot check the results: an agent can make a systematic error that its own summary will not reveal.
- Integrate the changes only after they hold together.

## Gates

- **Independence before dispatch.** Every domain is understood without context from the others and shares no state. Related or shared-state work is not parallelized.
- **One domain per agent.** A prompt covers a single problem domain, not several.
- **Self-contained prompts.** Each agent gets all the context it needs, since it does not inherit the coordinator's session. Name every input by path or quote it. Never point at context the receiving agent cannot see ("the file we discussed", "as above", "continue the plan").
- **Constraints are stated.** Each prompt names what the agent must not change.
- **Parallel dispatch.** Once independent work is ready and authorized, dispatch the full ready set together; use batched tool calls for bounded queries.
- **Integrated and verified afterward.** The results are reviewed, checked for conflicts, and run against the full suite before they are accepted.

## Anti-patterns

- Parallelizing related failures that one fix might resolve together.
- Fanning out tasks that share state, so agents interfere with each other.
- Splitting a task that needs full-system context into domains that cannot stand alone.
- Dispatching speculative implementation before enough investigation to establish independence; do bounded investigation, then reassess parallel work.
- Sending a broad prompt such as "fix all the tests" instead of one focused domain.
- Omitting the context, so an agent cannot understand the problem on its own.
- Leaving constraints implicit, so an agent refactors beyond its scope.
- Accepting summaries without checking for conflicts or running the full suite.

  English, plus a short explanation of what changed so the user learns. Use

  draft an English message, email, Slack/Teams message, PR comment, or reply —
  especially when the input or the request itself is in Portuguese ("melhore
  esse texto", "escreve um email pedindo...", "revisa meu inglês") or a

---

# English Writing Assistant for Portuguese Speakers

Built for Brazilian Portuguese native speakers who want to write clearer, more
natural English. The user may hand you a finished draft, a rough idea, or a few
bullet points — in Portuguese, English, or any mix. The output is always a
polished English message plus a brief explanation of the changes.

## Phase 1 — Understand the input

Read what the user shared and identify:

- **The material**: a draft to improve, or bullets/an idea to turn into a message.
- **Tone**: professional, casual, friendly, formal. Infer from context; ask only
  if it's genuinely ambiguous *and* the answer would materially change the output.
- **Audience and goal**: a colleague, manager, customer, team channel — and
  whether this is a request, update, apology, question, or report. Infer when you can.

If the user gave only bullets or a rough idea (not a full draft), write the
message from scratch from their intent. If their instructions are in Portuguese,
understand them fully and proceed — the deliverable is still an English message
plus the explanation.

## Phase 2 — Improve the text

Rewrite with these priorities:

- Fix grammar, spelling, and punctuation.
- Replace unnatural phrasing (often literal translations from Portuguese) with
  idiomatic, fluent English.
- Match vocabulary and register to the intended tone and audience.
- Improve flow and clarity **without changing the meaning**.
- Keep the author's voice and personality — don't over-formalize or
  over-casualize unless that's the stated goal.
- Preserve technical terms, names, and specific details exactly as given.

## Phase 2b — When the text is an instruction

A runbook, a prompt, or a procedure gets a structural pass, borrowed from
Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100). There is no word limit here: cutting
words is not the goal, removing ambiguity is.

- Put each condition next to its action, in the same sentence.
- Write one instruction per sentence. Split a sentence that carries two
  instructions, or an instruction plus its exception.
- Keep every subject, verb, and article. The dropped word is where the
  ambiguity enters.
- Use one term for each concept in the document. Don't rotate synonyms.
- Use the verb, not its noun form: "analyze the log", not "perform an analysis
  of the log".
- Use a numbered list for a sequence, and a list for a set of conditions.
- Keep every hedge at its original strength. "May", "unless", and "prefer" carry
  the author's confidence, and promoting one to a fact changes the claim.

These rules apply when the reader cannot ask a follow-up question. For a human
reader, keep the author's voice.

## Phase 3 — Explain the changes

After the rewrite, briefly explain what changed and why — in plain language,
3–5 bullets max. Focus on **patterns the user can reuse** (e.g. "in English we
usually front the request, not the context"), not an exhaustive line-by-line
diff. The point is that they learn, not just copy-paste.

Write this explanation in the language the user used to ask you (Portuguese or
English) — match their preference naturally.

Optionally offer 1–2 alternative phrasings when there's a meaningful stylistic
choice they might prefer.

## Output format

Always print the rewritten message inside a fenced code block so the user can
copy-paste it in one click. Never use blockquotes (`>`), bold, or other inline
markdown inside the message itself — keep it as plain text ready to paste.

````
✏️ Improved version:

```
[The full rewritten message — plain text, no markdown]
```

What changed:
- [Change 1 — brief reason]
- [Change 2 — brief reason]
- [Change 3 — brief reason]

Alternative phrasing (optional):
- [Alternative, if relevant]
````

## Key principles

- **Preserve meaning** — never add, remove, or assume information the user didn't
  provide. If a bullet is genuinely unclear, ask rather than invent.
- When tone is uncertain, lean toward clear and professional.
- If the original is already good, say so and offer only light polish — don't
  rewrite for the sake of rewriting.
- The output message is always in English; the explanation follows the user's language.

name: finishing-a-branch
description: Use when implementation is complete and the tests pass and the branch needs to be landed, kept, or discarded. Trigger on requests to finish, merge, land, or open a PR for a branch, and on the question of what to do with completed work. Do not use before the work is done or while tests are failing.
---

# Finishing a Branch

Land completed work safely, or leave it deliberately in place. Verify tests, detect the environment, present the landing menu, execute the human's choice, then clean up only what this workflow owns.

## Overview

Finishing a branch is a decision, not a reflex. The work is done and the tests pass, and now the branch has to be merged, published as a PR, or kept as-is. The human owns that decision, so the agent presents a fixed menu and waits. Two rules keep the path safe: nothing is merged until the suite is green on the tree being integrated, and nothing is discarded or force-deleted without an explicit typed confirmation. The environment shapes the menu and the cleanup, because a branch may live in a normal checkout, a linked worktree, or a detached HEAD that belongs to the host.

## When to Use

- Implementation is complete and the tests pass.
- The user asks to finish, land, or merge a branch, or to open a PR for it.
- The user asks what to do with completed work, or explicitly asks to keep or discard it.
- A local merge is about to happen and the merged result needs verifying before cleanup.

Do not use before the work is done, or while the suite is failing: the menu comes after a green run.

## Process

### 1. Verify the tests first

Run the project's full test suite on the tree you are about to integrate. If it is red, report the failures and stop. Nothing lands until the suite is green, and a green run only proves the tree it ran on.

### 2. Detect the environment

Determine where the branch lives, because it selects the menu and the cleanup:

- **Normal repo**: the git dir and common dir are the same. Standard menu, no worktree to clean up.
- **Linked worktree on a named branch**: the git dir differs from the common dir. Standard menu, with worktree cleanup possible.
- **Detached HEAD**: `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` returns `HEAD`, so no branch is checked out. This can happen in a normal checkout as well as a linked worktree. Reduced menu, with no local merge; the workspace is externally managed, so leave it in place.

Capture the worktree path now, before any step changes directory.

### 3. Determine and confirm the base branch

The base is what the work forked from, usually named in the conversation, a plan, or the branch's upstream. If it is not already known, ask, and confirm before merging. Merging into the wrong base is expensive to undo.

### 4. Present the landing menu

Present the options and wait; integration is the human's decision.

```
Implementation complete. What would you like to do?

1. Merge back to <base-branch> locally
2. Push and create a Pull Request
3. Keep the branch as-is (I'll handle it later)

Which option?
```

On a detached HEAD, offer the reduced menu: push as a new branch and open a PR, or keep as-is. Do not offer a local merge.

Discarding is not on the menu. It happens only when the human explicitly asks for it, and only through the confirmation in step 5.

### 5. Execute the choice

**Merge locally.** From the main repo root, check out the base, update it, and merge the feature branch. Then run the tests on the merged result. If they are red, stop, leave the worktree and branch in place, and investigate: nothing has been pushed, so the merge is local and recoverable. Only once the merged result is green, clean up the worktree and delete the branch with a safe delete.

**Push and open a PR.** Push the branch to the remote, naming a new branch if the HEAD is detached. Create the pull request against the base with the forge's tooling, following the repo's template and conventions if present, and report the URL. Keep the worktree: PR feedback gets fixed there.

Write the PR body in three parts:

- **Summary**: the smallest view that makes the key point clear, such as a diff sketch, a call tree, a short file tree, or a small diagram.
- **Evidence**: concrete proof the change works, before and after. Prefer a test run or console output; screenshots when the change is visual.
- **Merge Danger**: whether this is a one-way or a two-way door, and the blast radius if it goes wrong.

End with an explicit call on whether the change is safe to merge, and why.

**Keep as-is.** Report the branch name and the worktree path, and stop. The worktree is preserved.

**Discard (explicit request only).** This path exists only because the human asked to throw the work away. Confirm first, listing exactly what will be permanently deleted: the branch, its commits, and the worktree. Wait for the typed confirmation before doing anything. Then clean up the worktree and force-delete the branch.

### 6. Clean up the workspace

Cleanup runs only for a local merge and for a confirmed discard; push-and-PR and keep-as-is always preserve the worktree. Remove the worktree from outside it, using the path captured in step 2.

- **Normal repo**: nothing to clean up.
- **Worktree**: worktrees may be host-owned. If the host provides a worktree tool, use it. Remove a worktree only when this workflow owns it, never on a guess.
- **Removal refused**: a refusal means the worktree holds files that exist nowhere else. Never force-remove on your own initiative. Show the human what is at stake and ask before proceeding.
- **Otherwise**: the host owns the workspace, so leave it in place.

## Gates

- **Tests green before the menu.** A failing suite stops everything; nothing lands from a red branch.
- **The human picks the landing.** Present the menu and wait; never decide integration for them.
- **Base branch confirmed before merging.** Do not merge into a guessed base.
- **The merged result is verified before cleanup.** A red merged result stops the merge, and the branch and worktree stay in place.
- **Discard needs an explicit typed confirmation.** The human's request starts it; the typed confirmation authorizes it. No confirmation, no deletion.
- **Never force-delete or force-remove on your own initiative.** A refusal or a rejected push is investigated and shown to the human, never forced.
- **Clean up only what this workflow owns.** Worktrees may be host-owned; leave the rest alone.
- **The PR states whether it is safe to merge.** The body carries the Summary, Evidence, and Merge Danger, and an explicit merge call.

## Anti-patterns

- Presenting the menu before the suite is green, or merging a red branch.
- Choosing a landing option for the human, or treating obvious intent as consent.
- Merging into an unconfirmed base.
- Cleaning up the worktree or deleting the branch before the merged result is verified.
- Offering discard on the menu, or acting on "yeah, get rid of it" instead of the typed confirmation.
- Force-deleting a branch, or force-removing a worktree, to finish cleanup.
- Cleaning up a host-owned worktree because it looks stale.
- Force-pushing after a rejected push instead of investigating.
- Removing the worktree on PR feedback that is still being addressed.

name: handoff
description: Use when you want to compact the current conversation into a portable handoff document that another session (or you, later) can resume from. Trigger on requests to hand off, write a handoff, summarize where we are, or capture state for a fresh session.
---

# Handoff

Compact the current conversation into one portable document a fresh session can resume from with no other memory. Keep it concise and self-contained, and write it where the user can reach it.

## Overview

A handoff is a snapshot of work in progress, written for a reader who was not here. It carries the essentials another session needs: the current state, the decisions made and why, the threads still open, the immediate next action, and pointers to the files, paths, and commands involved. It is not a transcript and not a restatement of artifacts that already exist on disk. Reference those by path instead.

## When to Use

- The user wants to hand the current work off to another session, or to a later one.
- The user asks to summarize where things stand, or to capture state before pausing.
- Context is about to run out and the work needs to survive into a fresh conversation.

## Process

### 1. Choose where it goes

Write the document to a portable location the user can reach. A path the user names always wins. Otherwise use a gitignored or temporary location — the OS temp directory, or a path you have confirmed is gitignored (`git check-ignore <path>`). Never write it to the repository root, into a dev-only internal directory such as `skill-sources/`, or to any tracked path: the document can carry sensitive context and must not be committed by accident.

### 2. Capture the essentials

Record only what a fresh session needs to continue:

- **Current state**: what is done, what is in progress, and where the work stands.
- **Decisions made and why**: each choice that constrains the work, with its reason.
- **Open threads and questions**: what is unresolved, and what is still being decided.
- **Immediate next action**: the single thing to do next.
- **Pointers**: the files, paths, commands, and artifacts involved.

### 3. Reference, do not duplicate

Name existing artifacts by path or URL: specs, plans, commits, diffs, issues. Do not copy their content into the handoff.

### 4. Redact sensitive information

Remove API keys, passwords, tokens, and personally identifiable information before writing.

### 5. Write it and report the path

Save the document, then tell the user exactly where it was written so they can pass it to the next session.

## Gates

- **Portable location.** The document lands at a path the user can reach — a user-named path, or failing that a gitignored or temporary location — never the repository root, `skill-sources/`, or any tracked path.
- **Self-contained.** A fresh session with no memory of this conversation can resume from the document alone.
- **Essentials present.** State, decisions and why, open threads, the immediate next action, and pointers are all captured.
- **Secrets redacted.** No keys, passwords, tokens, or personally identifiable information.
- **Concise.** It reads as a snapshot, not a transcript.

## Anti-patterns

- Writing the handoff to the repository root, into `skill-sources/` or another dev-only internal directory, or to any tracked path.
- Dumping a transcript instead of distilling the essentials.
- Restating artifacts that already exist instead of pointing to them by path.
- Omitting the decisions and the reasons behind them.
- Leaving the next action vague or implicit.
- Including secrets or personally identifiable information.

name: improve-codebase-architecture
description: Use when explicitly invoked to survey a codebase for structural improvements. Trigger on requests to review a codebase's architecture, find deepening opportunities, or surface structural friction. Do not use for routine implementation, and do not refactor as part of the survey.
---

# Improve Codebase Architecture

Survey the codebase for **deepening opportunities** and report them as a prioritized list. The aim is testability and navigability: turn shallow modules into deep ones. Propose the changes; let the human choose which to make.

## Overview

Architectural friction shows up as modules that are hard to understand, hard to test, or hard to change safely. This skill finds that friction and names the **deepening opportunity** behind it: a refactor that moves behavior behind a smaller interface, at a clean seam. For the vocabulary (module, interface, seam, adapter, depth), see the `codebase-design` skill.

The output is a prioritized list, not a refactor. Every candidate states the concrete change and its payoff in terms of locality, leverage, and testability. The survey is read-only: it reads the code, and it never edits it. The human picks what to tackle.

## When to Use

- You are explicitly asked to review a codebase's architecture.
- You want deepening opportunities found and ranked.
- You are looking for shallow modules, leaky seams, or duplicated responsibility.
- You want a prioritized set of structural proposals before committing to any.

## Process

### 1. Scope before you scan

Deepening pays off by making future change easier, so weight the parts of the codebase that change most. If the user named a direction (a module, a subsystem, a pain point), take it and skip the inference. Otherwise walk back a good stretch of `git log --oneline` to find the hot spots, the files and areas that keep coming up, and let those pull attention first. If changes are scattered with no clear hot spot, widen the net.

### 2. Walk the codebase and note friction

Explore organically; do not follow rigid heuristics. Note where you experience friction:

- Where does understanding one concept require bouncing between many small modules?
- Where are modules **shallow**, with an interface nearly as complex as the implementation?
- Where have pure functions been extracted for testability while the real bugs hide in how they are called (no **locality**)?
- Where do tightly coupled modules leak across their seams?
- Which parts are untested, or hard to test through their current interface?

Apply the **deletion test** to anything you suspect is shallow: would deleting it concentrate complexity, or just move it? "Concentrates" is the signal.

### 3. Shape each candidate

For every candidate, write:

- **Files**: the files and modules involved.
- **Problem**: why the current architecture causes friction.
- **Change**: the concrete structural change, in plain language.
- **Payoff**: how locality, leverage, and testability improve.
- **Recommendation strength**: `Strong`, `Worth exploring`, or `Speculative`.

If a candidate contradicts a recorded decision (an ADR), surface it only when the friction is real enough to warrant revisiting that decision, and mark the conflict clearly. Do not list every theoretical refactor a decision forbids.

### 4. Report a prioritized list

Order the candidates by recommendation strength, strongest first, and end with a **Top recommendation**: which one to tackle first and why. A visual report (an HTML file written outside the repo, with a before/after diagram per candidate) is a good default, but a clear structured list is enough. State where the report was written and hand the choice back to the human: "Which of these would you like to explore?"

### 5. Stop at the proposal

Do not design interfaces or make changes in this skill. Once the human picks a candidate, hand off to a design or refactor pass. The survey ends when the list is delivered.

## Gates

- **Read-only.** The survey reads the codebase and writes nothing into it. Any report lands outside the repo.
- **Propose, never auto-refactor.** The skill ends with a prioritized list and a question; the human chooses what to change.
- **Every candidate names the concrete change and its payoff.** A finding with no change or no payoff is not a candidate.
- **Candidates are prioritized.** Each carries a recommendation strength, and the list is ordered.
- **The deletion test is applied.** A module suspected of being shallow is checked by asking whether deleting it concentrates complexity.

## Anti-patterns

- Refactoring or editing code as part of the survey.
- Presenting an unranked dump of every possible change.
- A candidate with no concrete change, or no payoff.
- Naming structure with vocabulary the design pass owns instead of the terms this survey uses.
- Listing theoretical refactors that recorded decisions already forbid.
- Designing interfaces, or starting implementation, before the human chooses.

name: interview
description: Use when the user wants to align on design or requirements before implementation, or asks to stress-test a plan, decision, or idea. Trigger on requests such as "interview me", "grill me", or "let's align on the design", and on starting a feature, component, or project whose intent is still fuzzy. Do not use for quick, fully specified tasks.
---

# Interview

Turn a rough idea into a shared understanding before anything gets built. The interview maps the design as a tree, works it in rounds, and keeps implementation behind an approval gate.

## Overview

An interview is a relentless but friendly conversation. You map every open decision as a **design tree**: each decision branches into the decisions that hang off it. You ask the questions whose prerequisites are already settled, look facts up yourself, and attach a recommended answer to every question. The interview ends when nothing is left silently assumed and the user confirms you share an understanding.

## When to Use

- The user wants to align on design or requirements before implementation.
- The user asks to stress-test a plan, decision, or idea, or says "grill me".
- Work is about to start on a feature, component, or project whose intent is still fuzzy.

## Process

### 1. Size the work

Classify the work and say the size in plain words. The user can override it.

| Size | The full description | Then |
|------|----------------------|------|
| Spike | a throwaway build | learn from it and return to the interview |
| Bounded | the design, in chat | build it after approval |
| Architectural | a written spec | get the spec approved, then build |

A **spike** is a quick throwaway build, often the cheapest way to learn what the user wants or whether something works. Keep it labeled throwaway, and bring what it taught you back into the conversation. If the work grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

### 2. Map the design tree

List the decisions. Every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask now without guessing at answers you have not heard.

### 3. Work the frontier in rounds

Ask the whole frontier together in one round. Number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round. Their answers reshape the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock the questions that depended on them. A question whose answer depends on another question still open this round belongs to a later round.

Format a round like so:

```
Q1 - <question title>: <question body, possibly with choices>

> <your recommended answer>

---

Q2 - <question title>: <question body>

> <your recommended answer>
```

### 4. Look facts up yourself

Finding facts is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (files, code, tools, or the web), look it up instead of asking. Do not block the round on it: a running lookup is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait. Ask the rest of the frontier now. The decisions are the user's: put each to them and wait.

### 5. Confirm shared understanding

The interview is done when the frontier is empty and every branch has been visited. Play back the settled decisions in the user's words, mark anything you are guessing as your guess, and ask what is wrong or missing. Only what the user confirms is theirs.

## Gates

- **No implementation before approval.** Writing product code, scaffolding, installing dependencies, and creating projects wait until the user approves the design. Reading and exploring are always fine.
- **A spike may be built** once the user approves it, and it stays labeled throwaway. Keeping what it produced is a new request that comes back through this gate.
- **Architectural work has a written spec.** The spec is the contract; the user approves it before implementation starts.
- **Act only after the frontier is empty** and the user confirms you share an understanding.

## Anti-patterns

- Asking the user for a fact you can look up yourself.
- Asking a question whose prerequisites are still open; it belongs to a later round.
- Sending the whole tree as one questionnaire instead of working the frontier in rounds.
- Starting to build before the design is approved.
- Treating a spike's output as the product.
- Filling gaps silently instead of surfacing them as questions with a recommended answer.

name: prototype
description: Use when a design question needs runnable code to answer, before committing to an approach. Trigger on uncertainty about whether a state model or piece of logic feels right, what an interface should look like, or which of several approaches to take, when the answer is cheaper to find by building than by reasoning. Do not use to build production features.

# Prototype

A prototype is throwaway code that answers a question. The question decides the shape, and the artifact is disposable by design.

## Overview

A prototype exists to resolve a design uncertainty that reasoning alone cannot settle. Build the smallest artifact that answers ONE question, keep it out of the real code path, and let the answer inform the real implementation. The prototype is a probe, not a deliverable: once it has done its job it is deleted or clearly marked as throwaway. Prefer the cheapest thing that resolves the uncertainty; a throwaway script or a single file beats a scaffolded app.

## When to Use

- A design question needs runnable code to answer before you commit to an approach.
- You are unsure whether a state model or piece of logic feels right in practice.
- You need to see what an interface could look like before choosing one.
- The cost of building to find out is lower than the cost of reasoning it out.
- You want to compare approaches that are hard to judge on paper.

## Process

### 1. Name the one question

State the single design question the prototype answers. If it cannot be phrased as a question with an observable answer, it is not ready to prototype. One prototype answers one question; a second question is a second prototype.

### 2. Pick the cheapest shape

Choose the smallest artifact that answers the question. A logic or state question wants a tiny runnable harness that pushes the model through the awkward cases; a look-and-feel question wants a few quick variations of the thing. A throwaway script or a single file is usually enough. Build only what the question needs: no tests, no error handling beyond what makes it runnable, no abstractions.

### 3. Keep it out of the real code path

Place the prototype where its context is obvious but a casual reader sees it is disposable, and keep it off the production path. Never let the prototype's code, files, or wiring become the real implementation. For an interface, follow the project's existing conventions rather than inventing new structure; for state, keep it in memory unless the question itself is about persistence.

### 4. Make it trivial to run

One command, or one file to open, with no setup thinking required. A prototype that takes effort to start will not get used.

### 5. Surface what changed

After every action, render or print the full relevant state so the answer is visible rather than inferred. The prototype's job is to make the uncertainty observable.

### 6. Report what you learned

State the verdict and the question it settled. Fold the validated decision into the real code, and report the answer plainly, including what the prototype ruled out.

### 7. Delete it or mark it throwaway

Once the answer is captured, delete the prototype, or leave it clearly named and marked as throwaway. The real code path keeps only the validated decision, never the probe.

## Gates

- **One question per prototype.** A prototype that answers several questions answers none clearly.
- **Throwaway from the start, and marked as such.** A reader can tell it is a prototype, not production.
- **Out of the real code path.** No prototype code, file, or wiring becomes the implementation.
- **The cheapest thing that resolves the uncertainty.** Prefer the smallest artifact over a scaffolded app.
- **The learning is reported.** The verdict and the question it settled are stated, not left implicit.
- **Deleted or clearly marked throwaway when done.** The real code keeps only the validated decision.

## Anti-patterns

- Building a prototype that answers no question, or several at once.
- Letting prototype code drift into the production path.
- Polishing: adding tests, abstractions, or error handling the question does not need.
- Choosing an elaborate scaffold when a single file would answer it.
- Leaving an unmarked, half-built prototype in the tree.
- Capturing the answer only in the prototype instead of reporting it.

description: Use when you need cited findings from primary sources (official docs, source code, upstream repos, specs, first-party APIs) to settle a factual question before deciding or designing. Trigger on requests to research a topic, gather docs or API facts, or verify a claim. Do not use when the answer is already settled or the question is a matter of opinion.

# Research

Settle a factual question with evidence, not recall. Dispatch the reading to a background subagent so the main thread keeps working, then return structured findings where every claim traces to the primary source that owns it.

## Overview

Research answers a factual question that blocks a decision or a design. The output is not an essay: it is a structured set of findings, each cited to a **primary source**. A primary source is the artifact that owns the claim (the official docs, the source code, the spec, the first-party API), never a secondary write-up of it. Established fact and inference stay visibly separate, and anything that could not be verified is said so plainly.

## When to Use

- A factual question blocks a decision, a design, or an implementation.
- You need docs or API facts gathered, or reading legwork delegated.
- You want a claim verified before relying on it.
- The answer must be traceable to a source, not taken on recall.

## Process

### 1. State the question

Turn the topic into the specific factual questions that would settle it. Name, for each, what evidence would count as an answer. A question with no observable answer is not research.

### 2. Dispatch a background subagent

Hand the search to a background subagent so the main thread keeps working while it reads. Give it the question and the source strategy, and ask for findings, not prose.

If the harness has no background subagent, **degrade to a foreground lookup**: do the same search yourself and return the same structured findings. Never skip the research or fail because the background path is unavailable.

### 3. Investigate primary sources

Read the artifact that owns each claim: official docs, source code, upstream repositories, specifications, first-party APIs. Follow every claim back to that owner. A secondary write-up is a lead, not a source.

### 4. Cite every claim

Attach a primary source to every claim, as a URL or a file path. A claim with no source is not a finding.

### 5. Separate fact from inference

Mark what the source establishes as fact, and mark your own reasoning as inference. Never let inference wear the clothes of established fact.

### 6. Return structured findings

Report the answer as a structured list of claims, each with its source and its fact/inference label. State plainly what could not be verified, and why. Do not bury the result in prose opinion.

## Gates

- **Every claim has a primary source.** No source, no finding.
- **Fact and inference are labeled.** Inference is never presented as established fact.
- **Unverified is stated as unverified.** A question that could not be answered is reported, not dropped.
- **Degrade, do not fail.** With no background subagent, run the lookup in the foreground and return the same findings.

## Anti-patterns

- Citing a secondary write-up instead of the source that owns the claim.
- Returning uncited claims or prose opinions.
- Presenting inference as established fact.
- Silently dropping a question that could not be verified.
- Skipping the research, or failing, when no background subagent is available.
- Answering from recall when a primary source is reachable.

name: retro
description: Use when explicitly invoked after a session to improve the agent's working environment from what slowed the work down. # Retro

A retrospective turns the friction of a finished session into small, concrete changes to the environment the next session runs in.

## Overview

A retro looks back at one session and asks what slowed it down. The output is not a report and not a verdict on the work: it is a short list of proposed changes to the working environment, each one minimal and tied to a specific friction the session hit. An environment change is an instruction, a script, a check, a skill, or a default. The skill **proposes** those changes; the user decides which to accept. It never edits steering files, policy, or defaults on its own, and it needs no tracker or ticket to operate.

## When to Use

- The user invokes `@retro`, or asks for a retrospective on a session.
- A session finished and something about the environment made it slower or rougher than it needed to be.
- The user wants a session's friction turned into concrete environment changes.
- You want to propose improvements to instructions, checks, scripts, skills, or defaults.

Do not use this mid-task: it reviews a session after the fact, not the code under change. It is not a general code review.

## Process

### 1. Pick the session

Use the session the user names. If none is named, use the current one. Read the primary sources for that session: the session log on this machine, plus the artifacts it touched.

### 2. Review what slowed the work down

Walk the session and note each point where it stalled, backtracked, or repeated itself. Look for friction the environment caused rather than mistakes in the work itself. A long hunt for a file, an error a check would have caught, a wrong turn a clearer instruction would have prevented.

### 3. Look for candidates

Consider the categories below, and read the repo's own setup before proposing anything, so a check that already exists but is unwired or silently broken is the finding rather than a reinvention.

- **Navigation**: was it hard to find the right files? Are there hidden dependencies between files? Would a pointer make it easier?
- **Automated checks**: could lint, typing, tests, or a filesystem linter have caught an error the agent made? Is there a guardrail (pre-commit hook or CI job running the repo's own check command)? A repo with no guardrail is itself a finding.
- **Coding standards**: should the reviewer be given a new rule, or an existing rule removed or clarified?
- **Steering files**: is `AGENTS.md` or another instruction file large or full of no-ops, so that some guidance belongs in standards or a check instead?
- **Tool economy**: were there expensive tool calls that a cheaper path could have avoided?
- **Information access**: was a crucial piece of information unavailable, and could access be added (dev-server logs, read-only access to a service)?

### 4. Classify each violation

A **mechanical** violation (a fixed syntactic pattern, a banned API, an import shape, a file-location rule) gets a deterministic check: a linter rule, a pre-commit hook, or a CI job, whichever is cheapest for this repo. Default to the check over the written rule. Reserve a coding-standards document for genuine **judgement calls** (cross-file consistency, "matches the surrounding style") that no check could substitute for.

### 5. Propose minimal changes

For each friction, state the smallest change that would prevent it next time. Prefer one instruction, script, skill, or default over a broad overhaul, and keep the change tied to the friction that motivated it. Say what the change is, where it goes, and why it helps. Order the proposals by severity.

### 6. Wait for acceptance

Present the proposals and stop. Do not apply a change, edit policy, or alter a default until the user accepts it. When the user accepts some, apply exactly those; leave the rest untouched.

## Gates

- **Proposed, not applied.** Changes are presented for the user to accept; nothing is altered silently.
- **Minimal and specific.** Each change is the smallest one that addresses a friction the session actually hit.
- **Environment, not the work.** The change targets instructions, checks, scripts, skills, or defaults, not the code that happened to be under the session.
- **Mechanical violations get a check.** Prefer a deterministic check over a written rule for anything a check can catch.
- **No tracker required.** The retro stands alone; no ticket, issue, or tracker step is needed.
- **Ordered by severity.** The most consequential friction is addressed first.

## Anti-patterns

- Editing steering files, policy, or defaults without asking.
- Proposing a broad overhaul where one small change would do.
- Proposing a change with no friction behind it.
- Writing a rule where a deterministic check is possible.
- Turning the retro into a general code review or a verdict on the work.
- Requiring a tracker, ticket, or issue to record findings.
- Reporting friction without proposing what would prevent it next time.
